reason: The supplied upper construction is invalid because blocks C and E overlap at cell \((5,2)\). The repaired proof retains the valid incidence-counting lower bound and replaces the upper construction by a disjoint periodic family, with only a linear number of boundary additions.
text:
Let a potential triple be any three consecutive cells in one row or column. The blocks removed in any legal process are pairwise disjoint potential triples. If the process is terminal, every potential triple intersects a removed block; otherwise that triple could still be removed.

For the lower bound, first suppose \(n\ge 2\). There are
\[
T=2n(n-2)
\]
potential triples. A removed horizontal block intersects at most five horizontal potential triples: their left endpoints can range only from two positions before its left endpoint to two positions after it. Each of its three cells belongs to at most three vertical potential triples, in distinct columns, so the block intersects at most nine vertical triples. Thus it intersects at most \(5+9=14\) potential triples. The same bound holds for a vertical block.

Since every potential triple must intersect some removed block, any terminal process using \(m\) blocks satisfies
\[
14m\ge 2n(n-2).
\]
Consequently
\[
b(n)\ge \frac{n(n-2)}7=\frac17n^2-\frac27n.
\]
For \(n=1\), we have \(b(1)=0\), and this inequality still holds. Hence we may take \(c=2/7\).

For the upper bound, consider first the infinite square grid. For every row \(i\in\mathbb Z\) and every \(k\in\mathbb Z\), select the horizontal block
\[
P_{i,k}=\{(i,5k+i),(i,5k+i+1),(i,5k+i+2)\}.
\]
These blocks are pairwise disjoint. In each row, the cells not covered by them occur in gaps of exactly two consecutive cells, so every horizontal triple meets a selected block.

A cell \((i,j)\) is uncovered precisely when
\[
j-i\equiv 3\text{ or }4\pmod 5.
\]
If three cells in column \(j\), in consecutive rows \(i,i+1,i+2\), were all uncovered, then, writing \(x=j-i\pmod5\), we would have simultaneously
\[
x\in\{3,4\},\qquad x\in\{4,0\},\qquad x\in\{0,1\},
\]
which is impossible. Thus every vertical triple also meets a selected block.

Now restrict to the \(n\times n\) grid \(G\), retaining only those \(P_{i,k}\) lying wholly in \(G\). Call this finite family \(F\). In each row there are at most \(n/5+1\) such blocks, so
\[
|F|\le \frac15n^2+n.
\]
Let \(Q\subseteq G\) be a potential triple disjoint from all blocks in \(F\). In the infinite pattern, \(Q\) meets some \(P_{i,k}\). That block cannot lie wholly in \(G\), so it crosses the left or right boundary. Its cells that lie in \(G\) are therefore in one of the first two or last two columns. Since \(Q\) has length three, it follows that \(Q\) is contained in the boundary strip
\[
S=\{(i,j)\in G:j\le4\text{ or }j\ge n-3\}.
\]
This strip has at most \(8n\) cells.

Starting with \(F\), greedily remove any further available triple until none remains. Every added triple was already disjoint from \(F\), and hence is contained in \(S\). The added blocks are pairwise disjoint and each uses three cells of \(S\), so at most \(8n/3\) blocks are added. The resulting family is terminal and has at most
\[
\frac15n^2+n+ rac{8n}{3}= rac15n^2+ rac{11}{3}n
\]
blocks. Therefore
\[
b(n)\le \frac15n^2+ rac{11}{3}n.
\]
Thus the theorem holds for every positive integer \(n\) with \(c=2/7\) and \(d=11/3\).
